title: AIP-C01 Skill 1.5.6: Give Models a Standard Way to Search
html:
AIP-C01 Skill 1.5.6: Give Models a Standard Way to Search

A hands-on lab with tool calling, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and a retrieval API. Task 1.5, post 6 of 7.

[IMAGE: cover-1-5-6.png — alt: "Skill 1.5.6: A standard way for models to search"]

AIP-C01 Hands-on Labs · Domain 1 · Task 1.5: Design retrieval mechanisms for FM augmentation · Post 6 of 7. Hands-on lab, about 30 minutes.

Once search works, everyone wants it. The support chatbot wants it. An internal agent wants it. A developer's AI assistant in their IDE wants it. Another team's service wants it over HTTP. If each one gets its own copy of the search code, they drift apart: different filters, different result formats, different bugs. This skill is about one retrieval contract that every caller uses, exposed through the doors each kind of caller expects.

What AWS says

Skill 1.5.6: Create consistent access mechanisms to enable seamless integration with FMs (for example, by using function calling interfaces for vector search, Model Context Protocol [MCP] clients for vector queries, standardized API patterns for retrieval augmentation).

What it means in plain words

  • Function calling interfaces: describe search as a tool (name, description, JSON schema). The model decides when to call it; your code runs the search and returns the result.
  • MCP clients for vector queries: the Model Context Protocol is an open standard for offering tools to AI applications. Put search behind an MCP server and any MCP client can discover and call it.
  • Standardized API patterns: the same request and response shape everywhere, for example POST /retrieve behind API Gateway.

[IMAGE: t1-5-6-access.png — alt: "One retrieval contract, three front doors: function calling, MCP server, HTTP API, plus the Knowledge Bases Retrieve API"]

What we're going to do

  1. Define one contract: retrieve(query, k) returns {query, results: [{id, source, text, score}]}.
  2. Give it to Amazon Nova 2 Lite as a tool through the Converse API, and watch the model decide when to search.
  3. Serve the same function from an MCP server, and call it from an MCP client.
  4. Let the MCP client hand the discovered tool to a Bedrock model.
  5. Optional: expose it as an HTTP API with API Gateway and Lambda.

What you'll learn

  • How the Converse API tool loop works: toolConfig, toolUse, toolResult.
  • Why a tool's description matters as much as its code.
  • How MCP lets clients discover tools instead of hard-coding them.
  • How to keep every caller on one contract.

What you'll need

  • Time and cost: about 30 minutes, under US$0.05
  • Region: us-west-2
  • Access: Python 3.10+ with boto3 and mcp; Amazon Nova 2 Lite through the US inference profile; Titan Text Embeddings V2
  • Files: github.com/prasanth2006z/aip-c01-labs, folder domain-1/task-1.5/skill-1.5.6-retrieval-access, plus the shared folder

The lab

Step 1: The contract

retrieval_api.py is the only place search is defined. It holds the function, the tool name, the description and the input schema:

TOOL_NAME = "search_knowledge"
TOOL_DESCRIPTION = ("Search Acme Tools' policies, shipping, warranty and parts documents. "
                    "Use it for any question about returns, refunds, delivery, warranty or spare parts.")

def retrieve(query: str, k: int = 3) -> dict:
    k = max(1, min(int(k), 5))
    ...
    return {"query": query, "results": [{"id", "source", "text", "score"} ...]}

Notice the clamp on k. The contract, not each caller, enforces limits.

Step 2: Function calling

pip install boto3 mcp
python tool_calling.py

The tool loop in run_with_tools() is generic:

  1. Call converse with toolConfig listing the tool.
  2. If stopReason is tool_use, run each requested tool and send the results back as toolResult blocks.
  3. Repeat until the model answers, or stop after four turns.

Watch the three questions. The first triggers one search. The second (blade and delivery time) may trigger two searches, one per topic: the model is decomposing the question itself. The third (“What's a good way to sharpen garden shears?”) gets no search at all: the system prompt says to answer general questions directly, and the tool description says it covers policies and parts. That's the benefit of tools over always-retrieve: no wasted search, no irrelevant passages in the prompt.

Step 3: The same search as an MCP server

python mcp_client.py

mcp_server.py is a few lines with the MCP Python SDK. It wraps the same retrieve():

mcp = FastMCP("acme-knowledge")

@mcp.tool(name=api.TOOL_NAME, description=api.TOOL_DESCRIPTION)
def search_knowledge(query: str, k: int = 3) -> dict:
    return api.retrieve(query, k)

The client starts the server over stdio, asks what tools it has, and prints the name, description and schema it discovered. Then it calls the tool directly. Nothing about the tool is hard-coded in the client.

Step 4: MCP tools to a Bedrock model

python mcp_client.py --with-model

This time the client converts each discovered MCP tool into a Converse toolSpec and runs the same tool loop, forwarding each call to the MCP server. Any MCP client (Claude Desktop, an IDE, Amazon Q Developer, an agent built with Strands or AgentCore) could use this server the same way.

Step 5 (optional): HTTP API

Zip retrieval_api.py, ../shared/search.py and ../shared/corpus.json, create a Lambda function with handler retrieval_api.lambda_handler, and add an API Gateway HTTP API with route POST /retrieve. Any service can now send {"query": "...", "k": 3} and get the same result shape as the tool and MCP callers. API Gateway adds authentication, throttling and usage plans in front of it.

Where AWS fits

  • Knowledge Bases Retrieve: already a standard contract for anything with AWS credentials; your tool or MCP server can simply wrap it.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: turns existing APIs and Lambda functions into MCP-compatible tools for agents, without rewriting them.
  • Bedrock Agents: action groups and attached knowledge bases are the managed form of the same idea.

Common pitfalls

  • The model never calls the tool, or calls it for everything: the description is the instruction. Say what the tool covers and when to use it.
  • Endless tool calls: cap the number of turns, and make the description and results clear enough to stop on.
  • ValidationException on the second call: every toolUse needs a matching toolResult with the same toolUseId, in a user message.
  • Each caller with its own search code: filters and formats drift. Put limits and access checks in the contract.

Clean up

Nothing to delete unless you created the optional Lambda function and HTTP API.

What to remember

  • One retrieval contract; several front doors: function calling, MCP, HTTP.
  • The model should decide when to search → function calling (tool use) via the Converse API.
  • Many AI apps and agents need the same search → an MCP server; clients discover tools and schemas.
  • Other services need retrieval over HTTP → API Gateway + Lambda.
  • Existing APIs as tools for agents → AgentCore Gateway.
  • Cap tool-call turns; write tool descriptions as carefully as prompts.

The exam scenarios for this skill are in post 7 of this task: Task 1.5 Exam Notes.

References

  • Call a tool with the Converse API
  • Model Context Protocol
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
  • API Gateway HTTP APIs
